1. I make this statement in support of the Claimant's claim. The facts in it are within my own knowledge unless

2. I have lived at the address above since 1998. The Claimant, ⟦name|Halima⟧, moved into the ground-floor flat at
   No. 43 in March 2024. Our two houses share a back yard wall and a drain run. Everybody round here calls me
   ⟦name|Tam⟧, and that is how the Claimant knows me.

3. From about November 2024 I noticed black mould coming through the back bedroom wall of No. 43, which I could
   see from my kitchen window. ⟦name|Halima⟧ showed me the inside of the flat on 2 December 2024. The plaster under
   the window was soaking and you could smell the damp from the hall.

4. On 2 December 2024 I telephoned the Defendant's office on the Claimant's behalf because she was not confident
   on the phone in English at that time. I spoke to a woman who gave her name as ⟦name|Charlotte⟧. I told her about
   the mould and the length of gutter that had come away from the back wall. She said someone would come "within
   the fortnight". Nobody came.

5. I remember the evening of 14 January 2025 well because I was watching Andy Burnham being interviewed on the
   local news about the buses when I heard a loud crack from next door. I went round and part of the back bedroom
   ceiling had come down onto the cot. ⟦name|Halima⟧'s little boy, ⟦name|Tobi⟧, was in the front room with her at
   the time, thank God.

6. I took photographs on my phone that night and the next morning. I have given copies to the Claimant's
   solicitors, Prentice Hale Solicitors. The photographs are timestamped 14/01/2025 21:52 and 15/01/2025 08:10.

7. The Claimant gave me her mobile number, ⟦phone number|07700 900481⟧, so that I could ring her if anyone from the agency
   turned up while she was at work. Between January and April 2025 I saw a workman attend only once, on 3 March
   2025, and he stayed for less than twenty minutes. He told me he had "just been sent to have a look".

8. I am not related to the Claimant and I have no financial interest in the outcome of this claim.

I believe that the facts stated in this witness statement are true. I understand that proceedings for contempt

Dear ⟦name|Nurul Aina binti Kamarudin⟧,

You have applied for entry clearance to the United Kingdom as the partner of ⟦name|Daniel Whitcombe⟧, who you state
is present and settled in the UK, residing at ⟦street address|58 Thornbury Avenue, Shirley, Southampton SO15 5BS⟧. I have
considered your application under paragraphs EC-P.1.1 and E-ECP.2.1 to E-ECP.4.2 of Appendix FM and under
Appendix FM-SE.

THE DECISION
I have refused your application for entry clearance because:

Financial requirement
To meet the financial requirement under paragraph E-ECP.3.1, your partner must have a gross annual income of at
least £29,000. You have relied on your partner's salaried employment with Solent Freight Services Ltd (Category A).
Paragraph 2 of Appendix FM-SE requires payslips covering the 6 months before the date of application and a letter
from the employer confirming the employment, the gross annual salary and the length of employment.

You provided payslips for February, March, April, June and July 2026 only; no payslip for May 2026 was provided.
The employer's letter dated 12 August 2026, signed by ⟦name|Helen Marchetti⟧ (HR Advisor), states a salary of
£27,450 per annum, which is below the required level. The P60 for the tax year 2025/26 issued to your partner under
National Insurance number ⟦tax id|JX 63 81 27 D⟧ shows gross pay of £26,980.

I have also considered whether you could meet the requirement using cash savings under Category D. The Nationwide
statements provided for the account ending ⟦account number|4416⟧ show a balance of £3,812.14, which is below
£16,000 and cannot be counted.

I am therefore not satisfied that you meet the requirements of paragraph E-ECP.3.1.

Relationship requirement
I am satisfied that you and your sponsor are in a genuine and subsisting relationship and intend to live together
permanently in the UK. I have noted the marriage certificate (Selangor, 14 February 2025) and the substantial
evidence of contact. This requirement is met.

English language requirement
Met - IELTS Life Skills A1, test reference 25MY004188.

Exceptional circumstances
I have considered, under paragraphs GEN.3.1 and GEN.3.2 of Appendix FM, whether there are exceptional
circumstances which would render refusal a breach of Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights because
it would result in unjustifiably harsh consequences for you, your partner or a relevant child. Your partner may
continue to visit you in Malaysia, as he did in 2024 and 2025, and you may reapply with the specified evidence.
I have found no such circumstances.

Your application is refused under paragraph EC-P.1.1(d) of Appendix FM.

YOUR RIGHT OF APPEAL
You may appeal against this decision under section 82(1)(b) of the Nationality, Immigration and Asylum Act 2002
on the ground that the decision is unlawful under section 6 of the Human Rights Act 1998. Your notice of appeal
must be received by the First-tier Tribunal (Immigration and Asylum Chamber) no later than 28 days after the date
you received this notice.

I have reviewed your application for permanent residence and the documents submitted in support of it. I have
concerns that you may not meet the requirements of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) and the
Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR), and that you may be inadmissible to Canada under paragraph
40(1)(a) of IRPA for misrepresentation.

In your Express Entry profile and application you declared 14 months of full-time skilled work experience as a
Quality Assurance Analyst (NOC 21222) with Lakeshore Digital Systems Ltd. in Toronto, from March 2024 to May 2025.
The employment reference letter you submitted, dated June 3, 2025, is signed by ⟦name|Marcus Lindqvist⟧,
identified as Director of Engineering.

Verification undertaken by this office indicates that:
  - the telephone number shown on the letterhead is not in service;
  - your Notice of Assessment for 2024 (SIN ending ⟦tax id|***-***-418⟧) reports employment income of $11,240,
    which is inconsistent with the declared annual salary of $68,500; and
  - Mr. ⟦name|Lindqvist⟧ advised an officer by telephone on September 10, 2026 that he did not sign the letter and
    that you worked for the company on a part-time contract for approximately four months.

Under subsection 16(1) of IRPA, a person who makes an application must answer truthfully all questions put to
them and must produce all relevant evidence and documents that the officer reasonably requires.

Paragraph 40(1)(a) of IRPA provides that a permanent resident or a foreign national is inadmissible for
misrepresentation for directly or indirectly misrepresenting or withholding material facts relating to a relevant
matter that induces or could induce an error in the administration of the Act. A person found inadmissible under

     CALDERWOOD, J. - ⟦name|Arjun Mehta⟧ appeals the trial court's final parenting plan, which limited his
residential time under RCW 26.09.191(3) and gave ⟦name|Leah Rosenthal⟧ sole decision-making authority over
education. ⟦name|Mehta⟧ contends the court abused its discretion by adopting the parenting evaluator's
recommendations without finding that his conduct had an adverse effect on the child's best interests. We affirm.

                                      FACTS
     ⟦name|Rosenthal⟧ and ⟦name|Mehta⟧ married in 2015 and have one child, ⟦name|N.M.⟧, born in 2017.(1) ⟦name|Rosenthal⟧
petitioned for dissolution in King County Superior Court in March 2023. The court appointed Dr. ⟦name|Hana Kowalski⟧,
a licensed psychologist, to conduct a parenting evaluation.

     ⟦name|Kowalski⟧ interviewed both parents, observed each of them with ⟦name|N.M.⟧, and spoke with the child's teachers
and therapist. Her report found that ⟦name|Mehta⟧ had on several occasions failed to return ⟦name|N.M.⟧ at the end of
his residential time, had twice withdrawn ⟦name|N.M.⟧ from school for extended trips to visit relatives in Pune
without ⟦name|Rosenthal⟧'s agreement, and had communicated with ⟦name|Rosenthal⟧ through the OurFamilyWizard
application in a manner the evaluator described as "persistently hostile and demeaning."

     After a four-day trial before Judge Denise Okamura, the court adopted most of the evaluator's
recommendations. It entered a parenting plan placing ⟦name|N.M.⟧ primarily with ⟦name|Rosenthal⟧, granting ⟦name|Mehta⟧
alternating weekends and one midweek dinner, and prohibiting either parent from removing the child from Washington
during the school year without written consent. ⟦name|Mehta⟧ appeals.

                                     ANALYSIS
     We review a trial court's parenting plan for abuse of discretion. A court abuses its discretion when its
decision is manifestly unreasonable or based on untenable grounds or reasons. We do not review the trial court's
credibility determinations or reweigh conflicting evidence.

     Under RCW 26.09.191(3), a court may limit any provision of a parenting plan if a parent's involvement or
conduct "may have an adverse effect on the child's best interests" and the court finds that a listed factor
exists, including "[t]he abusive use of conflict by the parent which creates the danger of serious damage to the
child's psychological development." RCW 26.09.191(3)(e).

     ⟦name|Mehta⟧ argues that the trial court made no express finding of adverse effect. We disagree. Finding of
Fact 2.12 states that "the father's repeated unilateral withdrawal of the child from school and his hostile
communications have caused the child significant anxiety, as reported by the child's therapist." That is a
finding of adverse effect, and it is supported by substantial evidence, including ⟦name|Kowalski⟧'s testimony and the
therapist's records admitted as Exhibit 41.

     ⟦name|Mehta⟧ also argues that the court erred by excluding the declaration of his sister, ⟦name|Priya Mehta-Rao⟧,
filed two days before trial. The court excluded the declaration as untimely under the case schedule and LCR 26.
Because ⟦name|Mehta⟧ offers no reason for the late disclosure and the declaration largely repeated his own testimony,
the court did not abuse its discretion.

     Affirmed.

                                     REASONS

Judgment having been sent to the parties on 24 June 2026, and written reasons having been requested by the
claimant in accordance with rule 60 of the Employment Tribunal Procedure Rules 2024, the following reasons are
provided.

Introduction
1.  The claimant, Mr ⟦name|Tomasz Kowalczyk⟧, was employed by the respondent as a warehouse operative, and later as
    a team leader, at its Coleshill distribution centre from 9 May 2016 until his summary dismissal on 14 November
    2025. He claims unfair dismissal under section 98 of the Employment Rights Act 1996 ("ERA") and notice pay.

2.  The respondent says the reason for dismissal was conduct, namely that on 29 October 2025 the claimant clocked
    in a colleague, Mr ⟦name|Dariusz Wąs⟧, using Mr ⟦name|Wąs⟧'s fob, when Mr ⟦name|Wąs⟧ was not on site, so that he was
    paid for a shift he did not work.

The evidence
3.  I heard evidence from the claimant and, for the respondent, from Mr ⟦name|Gareth Pryce⟧ (Site Operations Manager,
    who investigated), Ms ⟦name|Rachel Oyelowo-Hart⟧ (Regional HR Business Partner, who dismissed) and Mr ⟦name|Neil
    Chadha⟧ (Head of Operations, who heard the appeal). There was an agreed bundle of 312 pages and a set of CCTV
    stills.

Findings of fact
4.  The respondent operates a fob clock-in system at each gate. The clocking records (bundle p.118) show the fob
    assigned to employee number ⟦employee id|HP-20931⟧ (Mr ⟦name|Wąs⟧) presented at Gate 3 at 05:57:41 on 29 October
    2025, one second after the fob assigned to employee number ⟦employee id|HP-14077⟧ (the claimant).

5.  The still at p.121 shows one person at Gate 3 at that time. Mr ⟦name|Pryce⟧'s evidence, which I accept, is that
    the person is the claimant. The claimant did not dispute this at the investigation meeting.

6.  At the investigation meeting on 4 November 2025 the claimant said that Mr ⟦name|Wąs⟧ had given him the fob at the
    end of the previous shift because "⟦name|Darek⟧" was going to be late after a hospital appointment and had asked
    him to "sort it". The claimant accepted that he knew the respondent's clocking policy (p.64) prohibits using
    another employee's fob in any circumstances and that breach is listed as gross misconduct.

7.  Mr ⟦name|Wąs⟧ arrived on site at 09:40. He was paid from 06:00. He resigned before any disciplinary hearing.

The law
8.  Under section 98(1) and (2) ERA it is for the employer to show the reason for dismissal and that it is a
    potentially fair reason; conduct is such a reason (s.98(2)(b)). Under section 98(4) the question whether the
    dismissal was fair depends on whether, in the circumstances, the employer acted reasonably in treating it as a
    sufficient reason for dismissal, determined in accordance with equity and the substantial merits of the case.

9.  In a conduct case I apply the guidance in British Home Stores Ltd v Burchell [1978] IRLR 379: did the employer
    genuinely believe the employee was guilty of the misconduct, on reasonable grounds, after as much investigation
    as was reasonable? I must not substitute my own view for that of the employer; the question is whether
    dismissal fell within the band of reasonable responses.

Conclusions
10. The respondent genuinely believed the claimant had clocked in Mr ⟦name|Wąs⟧ knowing he was not on site. That
    belief was founded on the clocking data, the CCTV and the claimant's own account. The investigation was
    reasonable. Although the claimant had nine years' clean service, dismissal was within the band of reasonable
    responses for a deliberate breach that caused a financial loss to the respondent.

11. The claim of unfair dismissal is not well founded and is dismissed. As the claimant committed a repudiatory
    breach of contract, the claim for notice pay is also dismissed.

FACT SHEET - Tenancy List: getting ready for your hearing
Updated October 2026

Who this fact sheet is for
Landlords, tenants, agents and social housing providers who have an application listed in the Tenancy List under
the Residential Tenancies Act 2010 (NSW).

Your Notice of Hearing
Your Notice of Hearing shows your application number (for example RT 26/41187 or SH 26/09312), the date and time,
and whether the hearing is in person, by telephone or by video. Check the venue carefully. Tenancy List hearings
are held at Sydney (Level 10, John Maddison Tower, 86-90 Goulburn Street), Liverpool, Parramatta, Penrith,
Wollongong, Newcastle and at some regional courthouses.

Fees (from 1 July 2026)
  Tenancy application ............................................... $58 (concession $15)
  Application for a renewal of proceedings / set aside .............. $58
  Internal appeal to the Appeal Panel ............................... $637 (concession $159)
Social housing providers lodging in bulk should contact the Registry.

What to bring
Bring three copies of every document you want the Tribunal to consider: one for you, one for the other party and
one for the Tribunal Member. Useful documents include:
  - the residential tenancy agreement and the condition report (section 29);
  - the rent ledger or bank records showing rent paid;
  - termination notices and proof of service (for non-payment of rent, at least 14 days' notice - section 88);
  - photographs, with the date they were taken;
  - quotes, invoices and receipts for repairs or cleaning;
  - Rental Bond Online claim details, including the bond number.

Conciliation
Most tenancy matters start with conciliation. A Tribunal conciliator will help you and the other party try to
reach an agreement. If you agree, the Member can make consent orders under section 59 of the Civil and
Administrative Tribunal Act 2013. If you cannot agree, your matter will usually be heard on the same day.

If you cannot attend
Contact the Registry as soon as possible. If you do not attend, the Tribunal may hear and decide the application
in your absence. You can apply to set aside an order made in your absence within 14 days.

Interpreters
Interpreters are free. Tell the Registry which language you need when you lodge or as soon as you receive your
Notice of Hearing.

Getting help

  NSW Fair Trading - 13 32 20
